# code


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

An index built for prose is a poor fit for source code. The useful units
of code are functions and classes. The useful names are identifiers.
What matters is which function calls which.
[kosha](https://github.com/vedicreader/kosha) is the code index of the
vault. It splits source files into functions and classes with their
syntax tree. It embeds them with a model trained on code. It builds a
call graph in which each symbol has a PageRank score, a measure of how
central the symbol is. kosha keeps its index in `.kosha/` inside the
repository. It does not keep the index in the vault file.

`index_code(dir)` builds or updates that index. Later calls index only
the files that changed. `code_search` searches the index. `symbol(name)`
returns one function or class with its file, PageRank, callers and
callees. `where_to_add(description)` ranks the places in the repository
where a described change belongs.

`grep(pattern)` runs [ripgrep](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep)
over the files on disk, through
[rgapi](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/rgapi). It finds exact text. It
also searches files that kosha never indexed and files that changed
since the last `index_code`. It respects `.gitignore`.

### Combining the three searches

`federate(q)` runs several searches at once. Each search is called a
leg. The legs are the prose of the vault, each other shelf, the kosha
index of the repository (and of installed packages with `env=True`), and
ripgrep. The vault and kosha use different embedding models, and ripgrep
uses no model. Their scores cannot be compared. `federate` merges the
legs by rank with reciprocal rank fusion, which needs only the order of
each leg. `weights=` favours one leg over another. Every hit has the
same fields: `source` (the leg), `ref`, `title`, `where` and `text`. It
also has `open`, which says how to open the hit. A leg that fails is
reported in `legs` and in `note`. The other legs still answer.

### Vault.federate

``` python
def federate(
    q:str, # the query
    limit:int=12, # fused hits returned
    prose:bool=True, # the vault's own documents, papers, notes
    repo:bool=True, # kosha's repo index
    env:bool=False, # kosha's installed-package index
    grep:bool=True, # ripgrep over the working tree
    kind:str=None, # restrict the prose leg to some KINDS
    shelves:bool=True, # other shelves as their own legs: True for all, a list to pick, None for none
    weights:dict=None, # per-leg RRF weights, e.g. {'prose':1.0,'repo':1.5}
    dir:str=None, # repo for the code and grep legs
    per_leg:int=None, # hits pulled from each leg before fusion
    *, pii:str='off', pii_ner:bool=False, stale:bool=False
)->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
```

*Search prose, other shelves, indexed code and the files on disk at
once, and merge the results by rank.*

### Code in an answer

When kosha has indexed the repository, `.kosha/code.db` exists. Then
`context` and `ask` add code hits after the prose sections (`code=4` by
default). A code hit has the same fields as a section. The prompt and
the citations treat both alike. A code hit has no `node_id`, because
`read` cannot open it. Its `filename` is `path:line` on disk.

## Try it

Each leg can be turned off. Each leg fails on its own. This example runs
only the prose leg.

``` python
v = Vault(':memory:')
v.note('litesearch fuses the FTS and vector legs with reciprocal rank fusion.')
f = v.federate('rank fusion', repo=False, grep=False)
f.hits[0].where, f.legs, f.note
```
